Chapter 3. Prompt Engineering with MLflow

Prompt engineering is often introduced as a creative exercise: find the right words, coax the model, celebrate when it answers correctly, and then pretend nothing will ever change again. In real systems, prompts behave less like poetry and more like product configuration with sharp edges. A small wording tweak can change whether your application asks for missing details, whether it over-promises policy exceptions, or whether it returns something the application can reliably parse.

That is why prompts deserve to be treated as first-class assets with a lifecycle. Mastering prompt engineering and end-to-end prompt lifecycle management is simple to state and surprisingly hard to execute consistently. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to design prompts that are stable under real-world input, manage them in a controlled system of record, measure whether a change helps or hurts, and roll improvements into production safely.

We will keep the scope intentionally focused. Chapter 1 established the core GenAI building blocks and our running example. Chapter 2 expanded that into a lifecycle mindset across development and production. Here in Chapter 3, we zoom in on the prompt itself and answer the practical questions teams run into immediately:

  • How do we write prompts that are clear, constrained, and robust to ambiguity?

  • How do we avoid the “copy, paste, and pray” workflow where the deployed prompt is whatever someone last edited in a notebook?

  • How do we update prompt behavior without redeploying the application every time a sentence changes?

  • How do we compare prompt versions objectively, instead of debating screenshots in chat?

  • How do we use automatic prompt tuning without turning our production assistant into a science project?

To do this, we lean on capabilities in MLflow on Databricks that are designed specifically for prompt lifecycle management: the MLflow Prompt Registry for storing and versioning prompts, aliases for safe promotion, and built-in workflows to evaluate and optimize prompt versions (see Figure 3-1). The thread running through all of these topics is repeatability. If you cannot reproduce a behavior, you cannot confidently improve it.

This chapter is structured as a progression from craft to operations. We start with prompt engineering fundamentals: core techniques, best practices, and antipatterns that cause instability and hallucinated confidence. Then we move into managing prompts with MLflow Prompt Registry: creating and editing prompts, publishing new versions, and making prompts discoverable for teams. Next, we show how to load and format prompts safely in code and how to integrate alias-based prompts into an application so that updating behavior is a controlled release action rather than a redeploy ritual. Finally, we cover how to compare prompt versions and apply automatic prompt optimization, always with the same principle: improvements must be measurable and reversible.

If you take away one idea from this chapter, let it be this: prompts are part of your production surface area. Treat them with the same care you treat code that touches customers.

Fundamentals of Prompt Engineering

Prompt engineering is about designing instructions that survive contact with real users, real ambiguity, and real constraints such as latency, cost, and downstream parsing. A prompt shapes what the model pays attention to, what it should ignore, how confident it should sound, and what form the output should take.

In the Unity Airways use case we discussed in Chapters 1 and 2, the difference between a “good” and “bad” prompt is less about style or artistry and more about tangible, operational results. A good prompt makes the model ask for missing booking details before claiming eligibility. It avoids inventing waivers. It produces an answer that a customer support agent could actually send without first rewriting it in panic.

This section gives you the foundations you will use throughout the chapter. We will keep the focus on prompt design itself, not on broader system design. Think of this as learning how to write instructions that are unambiguous, testable, and versionable so they can live in the MLflow Prompt Registry without turning into a fragile asset.

Core Prompting Techniques

You will see many naming conventions for different prompting techniques. The names are less important than the intent behind them. Each technique is just a way to reduce ambiguity and steer the model toward a consistent behavior.

Zero-shot prompting

Zero-shot prompting is the simplest form: you ask a question or provide a task with no examples. It is fast to write and often good enough for simple tasks such as summarizing a paragraph or answering a factual question when the model has enough context.

The risk is that zero-shot prompts leave too much room for interpretation. If the user asks, “Can I change my flight?” the model might answer confidently without asking the fare type, booking class, route, or timing. That is not the model being “bad.” That is the prompt failing to set boundaries.

Zero-shot works best when you do three things at once:

  • Define the role and scope (what the assistant is and is not responsible for).

  • Give clear constraints (length, tone, format).

  • Define what to do when information is missing.

A simple Unity Airways example might look like this:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Task: Answer the customer's question using only the information provided.
If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
Do not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.

Customer question: {{question}}

Write a concise answer (max 120 words).
"""
Tip

Notice the use of {{question}}. When you later store prompts in the Prompt Registry, Databricks uses the double-brace syntax for template variables.

Few-shot prompting

Few-shot prompting adds a small number of examples to guide the model’s behavior. It is especially useful when:

  • You need the model to consistently match a particular style.

  • You need a structured output format that is easy to alter.

  • The task has tricky edge cases that users phrase in unpredictable ways.

For Unity Airways, few-shot can be helpful for “policy-shaped” answers where the assistant must be careful with conditional language, for example, refunds, cancellations, missed flights, and schedule changes.

The trick is to keep examples short and representative. Do not try to cover every case within the prompt. That is what your evaluation dataset is for later. Your prompt examples should teach the format and the decision posture.

A good few-shot pattern is:

  • One example where the answer is direct

  • One example where the assistant must ask for missing details

  • One example where the assistant must decline to speculate

Keep the examples realistic. If your examples sound like they were written by a technical engineer who has never met a customer, the model learns that tone too. Business users who are closer to the end users would be more apt to provide natural-sounding examples. Here is an example related to the Unity Airways support assistant:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Goal: Help the customer with flight changes/cancellations/refunds.
Rules:
- If key details are missing, ask exactly ONE clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or eligibility. If policy depends on fare rules 
  and you do not have them, say what you need to confirm.
- Keep the final answer under 120 words.
- Use this structure:
  1) Answer/Guidance
  2) What I need from you (only if needed)

Customer question: {{question}}

Examples:
Example 1 (Direct answer)
Customer question: What are your customer support hours?
Expected response: Unity Airways customer support is available 24/7 for urgent 
                   travel issues. For general inquiries, response 
                   times may be slower during peak periods.

Example 2 (Ask for missing details)
Customer question: Can I change my flight to next week?
Expected response: You can often change a booking, but eligibility and any fees 
                   depend on your fare type and ticket rules. Can you 
                   share your booking reference?

Example 3 (Decline to speculate)
Customer question: Will I definitely get a full refund if I cancel today?
Expected response: I can’t confirm a full refund without checking your fare
                   rules, because refund eligibility and any cancellation fees 
                   depend on your ticket type and booking conditions. 
                   Could you share your booking reference?

Now respond to the customer question using the same style and rules.
"""

Reasoning prompts

You will often see “chain-of-thought” (CoT) used to describe prompts that request step-by-step reasoning. In practice, what you want in production is not the model’s full internal monologue. What you want is better decisions and fewer confident mistakes.

A safer pattern is to ask for a brief rationale that is either not shown to the user or shown as a short explanation. You can also ask the model to do its reasoning silently and output only the final answer. The point is to encourage deliberation without turning the customer response into a long ramble. For example:

  • “Consider what information is missing before answering.”

  • “If eligibility depends on policy details, ask a clarifying question.”

  • “Use cautious language when policy is not provided.”

You are not asking for a novel. You are asking for better judgment. Here is an example related to Unity Airways support assistant:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Goal: Provide a correct, policy-safe answer with minimal risk of overpromising.

Instructions:
1) First, think through what key information is missing that would change
eligibility (fare type, booking channel, route/date, disruption type, 
booking reference).
2) If key details are missing, ask exactly ONE clarifying question. Do not 
answer beyond what is safe without those details.
3) If details are sufficient, answer directly.
4) Do not invent fees, waivers, or refund eligibility. If policy is unclear, say 
what you need to confirm.
5) Keep the final response under 120 words.

Internal reasoning (do not reveal):
- List missing key details (if any)
- Decide: ask one question OR answer
- Identify any statements that would be speculation and avoid them

Customer question: {{question}}

Output (customer-facing only):
- If clarifying is needed: ask exactly ONE question.
- Otherwise: provide the answer in 2-4 short sentences.
"""

Self-correction and reflection

Models can contradict themselves, especially when prompts bundle multiple requirements. Self-correction patterns help, but they must be used carefully. You want reflection to improve quality, not to add another layer of uncertainty.

Two practical self-correction strategies:

Checklist pass

Ask the model to verify that it complied with constraints before returning the final answer. This works well for structural constraints like word count, JSON formatting, or required sections.

Error-focused revision

If you know common failure modes, tell the model to actively avoid them. For example: “Do not promise refunds without policy support.”

Here is a lightweight example:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Write the answer. Then verify:
- You did not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.
- You asked one clarifying question if key details were missing.
- The answer is under 120 words.

Return only the final answer.

Question: {{question}}
"""

This keeps the reflection internal and keeps the customer-facing response clean.

Prompt Engineering Best Practices

A prompt that works once is not the goal. A prompt that works when the user is vague, upset, or typing with one thumb on a moving train is the goal.

Let’s next look at some prompt practices that tend to matter most in real applications.

Be explicit about the job, scope, and boundaries

Start by defining what the assistant is doing. If the assistant’s job is “provide accurate steps and ask for missing details,” say that. If it should not provide legal advice or make eligibility promises, say that too. This prevents the model from filling gaps with invented certainty.

Here are some Unity Airways examples of boundary statements that help:

  • “If policy details are not provided, do not claim an exception.”

  • “If the question is about refunds, be cautious and ask for the fare type and booking reference.”

  • “If you are unsure, state what information is missing.”

This keeps tone specific and reduces drift.

Use constraints that are measurable

The model cannot reliably follow vague instructions like “keep it short” or “be professional.” Those instructions help, but they are not enough. Add constraints that are measurable and visible, like:

  • Maximum word count (or maximum sentences)

  • Output structure (e.g., sections with headings)

  • Output format (e.g., JSON with specific keys)

For customer support answers, limits on word count or restrictions on the number of sentences are more effective than “be concise.” A hard limit forces prioritization.

Use labels to separate inputs from instructions

Delimiters are one of the easiest and most underused reliability tools. They reduce the risk of prompt injection and make it easier for the model to separate “what I should do” from “what the user said.” Common delimiter patterns include triple backticks, XML-style tags, or clear separators like ---.

Here is a simple approach that works well for user messages:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Instructions:
- Answer using only the information in the customer message.
- If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.

Customer message: {{question}}

Write a concise answer (max 120 words).
"""

Even if a user says “Ignore previous instructions,” clearly separating the customer message from your system instructions makes it more likely the model treats that phrase as customer text, not a command.

Treat output format as a contract

If your application needs to parse the output, you should not rely on the model’s goodwill. You should define an output criteria in the prompt and keep it simple. For example, if your UI needs both an answer and a follow-up question, a JSON structure can reduce ambiguity:

template = """
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Return valid JSON with exactly these keys:
- "answer": string
- "clarifying_question": string or null

Rules:
- If key details are missing, put one question in "clarifying_question" and keep 
"answer" short.
- If nothing is missing, set "clarifying_question" to null.

Customer question: {{question}}
"""

This does not guarantee perfect JSON every time, but it improves consistency dramatically. Later, you can add stronger enforcement with downstream validation and retries, but the prompt is where you declare the contract.

Keep tone consistent, but do not let tone override correctness

Tone matters, but tone is not the mission. For customer support, the priority order is usually:

  1. Safety and correctness

  2. Policy compliance

  3. Clarity and helpfulness

  4. Tone and brand voice

If you promote “be cheerful and friendly” above “do not invent policy,” you will get friendly hallucinations, which are worse than blunt truth.

A practical way to prevent that drift is to treat tone as rules you can check, not an abstract personality. Table 3-1 shows how to translate vague tone requests into specific wording constraints. These constraints preserve voice while keeping correctness and compliance in control.

Table 3-1. Translating tone into testable wording constraints
Instead of this
(abstract tone instruction)		Use this
(specific, testable wording constraints)
“Be cheerful and friendly.”“Use calm, respectful language. Use a short greeting once. Avoid emojis and slang.”
“Sound empathetic.”“Acknowledge the user’s situation in one sentence (for example, ‘I can see why that’s frustrating.’). Then move to steps.”
“Be professional.”“Use neutral wording. Prefer short sentences. Avoid jokes, sarcasm, and informal fillers (for example, ‘totally,’ ‘no worries’).”
“Be confident.”“State what you know and what you don’t. Use ‘I don’t have enough information to confirm X’ instead of guessing.”
“Be reassuring.”“Explain the next step and expected outcome. Avoid absolute guarantees (avoid ‘definitely,’ ‘100%’).”
“Be concise.”“Limit to 5 bullets maximum. Put the recommendation first. Avoid repeating the user’s question.”
“Be thorough.”“Include: (1) decision, (2) rationale, (3) steps, (4) edge cases. Use headings and bullets.”
“Be humble.”“Avoid blame. Use ‘It looks like…’ for uncertainty. Don’t over-apologize (maximum one apology per reply).”
“Use brand voice.”“Use approved phrases only (provide three to five). Avoid inventing policy or making promises outside documented commitments.”
“Be firm.”“Use ‘I can’t help with that’ for disallowed requests, then offer allowed alternatives. No moralizing, no lecturing.”

Antipatterns and Debugging Habits

Prompt failures are often predictable. They fall into the following common categories, and once you see them, you start noticing them everywhere.

The “kitchen sink” prompt

This is the prompt that tries to do everything at once: summarize, classify intent, extract entities, cite policy, ask clarifying questions, and write in the voice of a hard-boiled detective.

Symptoms:

  • The model satisfies a few constraints and quietly drops the rest.

  • The output grows long, repetitive, or uneven.

  • The model sounds more certain than it should, because the prompt never states what takes priority when instructions conflict.

Fix:

  • Define one primary task and write the prompt around that outcome.

  • Convert secondary requirements into short, testable constraints.

  • Use structured output when fields must be present every time.

A good prompt should be a set of clear directives, not a battle plan for every possible outcome.

Vague instructions and untestable constraints

“Be accurate.” “Be professional.” “Be concise.” These are not wrong. They are just not enough.

If the prompt cannot be tested, it cannot be improved systematically. Replace vague requirements with measurable ones, and keep them in one place in the prompt so you can update them as a group.

Unchecked assumptions

If your prompt does not tell the model what to do when information is missing, the model will guess. That is how you get invented refund eligibility and phantom change fees. A well-designed prompt treats missing details as normal and requests them.

Overreliance on negative instructions

Negative instructions like “do not hallucinate” are not useless, but they are not sufficient. Models respond better when you tell them what to do instead. For example:

  • Instead of “Do not invent fees,” use “If fees are unknown, say you cannot confirm and ask for fare type.”

  • Instead of “Do not be verbose,” use “Use at most 120 words and include only the next steps.”

Changing multiple things at once

This is the fastest way to confuse yourself. If you change tone, output format, and policy wording in a single prompt revision, and the metrics move, you cannot tell what caused the change. You also lose the ability to reproduce the improvement, because you do not know which edit mattered.

A better iteration habit is to change one thing per version and record the hypothesis in the commit message. When performance improves or regresses, you can point to the exact part of the prompt responsible, such as a new constraint, a reordered priority, or a stricter output schema. This makes comparisons meaningful and helps you carry wins forward without accidentally undoing them when you create later versions down the line.

Managing Prompts with the MLflow Prompt Registry

If prompts are part of your production surface area, then storing them as random strings scattered across notebooks, jobs, and application repos is like running an airline where every gate agent keeps their own version of the boarding policy. It works right up until it does not, and the “incident review” is mostly people comparing screenshots.

The MLflow Prompt Registry fixes this by giving you a centralized, governed home for prompt templates, with versioning and promotion mechanics designed for real teams. It’s a Git-like model where prompts are named entities in Unity Catalog on Databricks, versions are immutable snapshots, aliases are mutable pointers to versions, and tags are version-specific metadata. That one paragraph captures the entire philosophy: prompts are not ad hoc text; they are managed assets.

The “Why” Behind the Registry

Teams adopt a registry when they hit a familiar pain point in which they can no longer answer basic questions reliably. For example:

  • Which exact prompt is running in production right now?

  • Who changed it, and why?

  • If the behavior regressed, what was the last known good version?

  • Can a domain expert update wording without opening a pull request against application code?

MLflow Prompt Registry is built for these workflows. It supports safe deployment with aliases such as production and staging for gradual rollout and rollbacks, and it allows collaboration through the UI so nonengineers can update prompts without editing code. It also sits within Unity Catalog, which means access control and auditing are handled consistently with the rest of your governed assets.

Tip

One practical implication matters early: you need the right Unity Catalog permissions. To view or create prompts in a UC–backed registry, you need CREATE FUNCTION, EXECUTE, and MANAGE privileges on the schema that stores prompts.

Prompt Registry SDK Overview

The registry exposes a small set of functions that cover the prompt lifecycle. Databricks summarizes the core functions as register_prompt() to create prompts or add new versions, load_prompt() to retrieve versions or aliases, search_prompts() to find prompts, set_prompt_alias() and delete_prompt_alias() to manage alias pointers, and deletion APIs for cleanup.

You do not need to memorize the API surface. You do need to internalize the lifecycle shape: create, version, promote, discover, and eventually retire. Figure 3-2 illustrates how MLflow Prompt Registry functions map to lifecycle stages.

A Tour of Prompt Lifecycle with Prompt Registry

The MLflow Prompt Registry provides a governed lifecycle for your prompt templates. In the following sections, we will walk through the key steps in this lifecycle: naming your prompt, creating the initial template, managing versions as you iterate, and using aliases to safely promote changes from development to production. We will also look at making prompts discoverable, searching prompts within UC, and deleting prompts.

Naming prompts and choosing a location

A prompt name is a Unity Catalog identifier, so the stable unit of organization is catalog.schema.prompt_name. This is worth treating like a standard. It makes prompt discovery and governance simple, and it avoids the “where did we store this” question.

Databricks also provides a convenient mechanism to link an MLflow experiment to a default Prompt Registry location: set an experiment tag called mlflow.prompt​Re⁠gistryLocation with the value catalog.schema. When set, MLflow GenAI APIs treat that Unity Catalog schema as the default namespace for prompt resolution, so fully qualified prompt names are not required. This helps teams maintain consistent governance and avoid accidental prompt registration in unintended schemas.

Here is a simple setup pattern you can reuse:

import mlflow
# Configure MLflow tracking and choose an experiment for your project
mlflow.set_tracking_uri("databricks")
mlflow.set_experiment("/Shared/unity-airways/unity-airways-prompts")

# Link this experiment to a default UC schema for prompts
mlflow.set_experiment_tags({
    # Set the Unity Catalog and schema for data and models before running this code
    "mlflow.promptRegistryLocation": f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}" 
})

That tag does not magically solve governance, but it sets a clear convention that your team can follow. The big win is consistency.

Creating prompts

Databricks supports creating prompts via the MLflow UI and via the Python SDK.

Creating prompts in the Databricks MLflow UI

The UI path is ideal when you want quick iteration, visibility, and input from nonengineers. The steps, in order, are:

  1. Navigate to an MLflow experiment.

  2. Open the Prompts tab.

  3. Select the catalog and schema.

  4. Create a prompt name.

  5. Create the first version and save it.

Note

Prompt Registry uses the {{variable_name}} syntax for template variables in the UI. That keeps prompt templates clean and makes them easy to render later with .format(...).

Creating prompts programmatically with the Python SDK

The SDK approach is ideal when you want repeatability, especially in shared notebooks, CI-like workflows, or demos where you need to bootstrap a workspace consistently.

Databricks’ quick start shows the essential workflow: register_prompt() creates version 1, then set_prompt_alias() assigns a production alias, and then load_prompt() retrieves it for use. The same example also highlights the double-brace template variables.

Here’s a Unity Airways example:

import mlflow

uc_prompt = "main.default.unity_airways_customer_support"

v1 = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name=uc_prompt,
    template="""\
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Rules:
- If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.

Customer question: {{question}}

Write a concise answer (max 120 words).
""",
    commit_message="v1: baseline support answer with safety and brevity constraints",
    tags={
        "use_case": "customer_support",
        "language": "en",
        "owner": "unity-airways-support",
    },
)
print(f"Created prompt {v1.name} version {v1.version}")

Note that register_prompt() creates a new prompt if the name does not exist; otherwise, it creates a new version under the same prompt name. register_prompt() accepts several parameters:

name (required)

The registry identifier for the prompt. On Databricks, this is typically a fully qualified Unity Catalog name such as catalog.schema.prompt_name, which keeps ownership and permissions explicit.

template (required)

The prompt content you want to version. This can be a plain string template that includes double-brace variables like {{question}}, or a structured chat template represented as a list of role/content message objects. Choose a string template for simple, single-turn prompts and a chat template when you want to separate system and user messages while versioning them together.

commit_message (optional)

A short, human-readable note describing the intent of this version. Treat it like a Git commit message for prompts. Make it specific enough so that in the future, you can understand what changed and why. For example: “Reduce refund overpromises by requiring fare type before eligibility statements.”

tags (optional)

Key-value metadata attached to the prompt version. Tags are for facts you want to filter or search on later, such as use case, language, owner, risk level, and the evaluation dataset used. Keep tag keys stable across versions so comparisons stay clean.

response_format (optional)

A schema describing the structure of the expected model output, provided as a Pydantic model or an equivalent schema dictionary. Use this when downstream code parses the output or when you want to enforce the presence of required fields.

model_config (optional)

Generation settings stored alongside the prompt version, such as the target model and decoding parameters. This is useful when you want reviewers to see both the template and its intended generation configuration as one versioned unit.

In practice, you will not use all the parameters all the time. Nevertheless, we recommend using optional parameters such as commit_message and tags to provide more information about the prompt version that you register.

After executing the previous Unity Airways code, you should be able to see that the first version of the prompt successfully registered within the MLflow Prompt Registry, as you can see in Figure 3-3.

This is intentionally simple. The prompt text itself will evolve, but the management pattern should stay stable.

Note

Prompt templates include placeholders written as {{variable}}. When your GenAI application uses the prompt, you populate these placeholders with runtime values. MLflow also provides to_single_brace_format() to convert templates to {variable} for frameworks such as LangChain or LlamaIndex that expect single-brace interpolation.

Once you have multiple versions, the UI also supports side-by-side comparisons (Figure 3-4). In Databricks, you can click the Compare button and select the versions to compare. This sounds like a convenience feature, but it changes how teams collaborate. Instead of debating “what changed,” you can point to an exact difference.

Versioning prompts

The registry is deliberately strict about version edits, as the prompt versions are immutable after creation. To edit a prompt, you need to create a new version.

At first, this can feel inconvenient. Then you realize why it matters:

  • Immutability makes comparisons meaningful.

  • It prevents accidental retroactive changes to what you thought you tested.

  • It turns rollback into a deterministic operation: “go back to version 3,” not “hope no one overwrote the prompt.”

Creating a new version programmatically simply involves calling register_prompt() again with the same prompt name and a new template. Databricks documents this directly: to create a new version, call mlflow.genai.register_prompt() with an existing prompt name.

Here is what a “small, intentional change” looks like:

import mlflow

uc_prompt = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support"

v2 = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name=uc_prompt,
    template="""\
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Rules:
- If the question is ambiguous, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- If the customer mentions refunds, do not promise eligibility without fare 
details.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.
- Keep the answer under 120 words.

Customer question: {{question}}

Answer:
""",
    commit_message="v2: tighten ambiguity handling and refund safety posture",
    tags={
        "change_type": "behavior",
        "risk": "medium",
        "hypothesis": "reduces overconfident refund promises",
    },
)

print(f"Created version {v2.version} of {v2.name}")

After executing this code, you should be able to see that two versions of the same prompt successfully registered within the MLflow Prompt Registry, as you can see in Figure 3-5.

Two habits make prompt versioning work long-term:

  • Commit messages should include intent. “Fix prompt” is not the intent. “Reduce refund hallucinations by requiring fare details” is the intent.

  • Change one major thing per version. If you change tone, structure, and policy phrasing all at the same time, you will not know what caused the improvement or regression.

To keep the practice disciplined, standardize a few lightweight conventions:

  • Use the format “behavior change | context | expected outcome” for examples (such as “Reduce refund overpromises | refunds | require fare type before eligibility statements”) and avoid vague descriptions (such as “Update prompt,” “Tweaks,” or “Fixes”).

  • Keep the version focused so you can attribute improvements or regressions to a specific edit.

  • Tag the change as micro, medium, or major so reviewers know what to expect.

  • Record a one-line hypothesis and tag operational risk as low, medium, or high, especially for sensitive areas like refunds, compensation, or safety.

  • Note whether the evaluation passed, which dataset you used, and a short intent tag, such as clarify_missing_details or no_speculation.

  • Keep consistent tags for use case, domain, language, owner, and team. Optionally, add rollout intent like target_alias=staging or release_candidate=true.

  • Tag it explicitly as a breaking change and list expected input variables if you rename template variables or change output format.

  • Capture a brief before/after note if latency or token growth matters.

Finally, keep prompt names stable and descriptive, and do not encode version numbers in the name. Let the registry history and aliases carry the versioning so comparisons and rollbacks stay clean.

Promoting via aliases

Aliases are how you turn “versioned artifacts” into “operational control.” An alias is a static string label that points to a specific prompt version, such as production or staging.

Unlike prompt versions, aliases are mutable. You can reassign an alias to a newer version without changing application code. That is the heart of safe prompt rollouts.

Setting an alias is a simple operation:

import mlflow
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(
    name="main.default.unity_airways_customer_support",
    alias="staging",
    version=2
)
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(
    name="main.default.unity_airways_customer_support",
    alias="production",
    version=1
)

This example mirrors the common pattern shown in the Prompt Registry examples, where one version is promoted to production and another is staged for testing. After executing this code, you should be able to see that staging and production aliases appear in prompt versions 2 and 1, respectively, in the MLflow Prompt Registry view.

set_prompt_alias() takes three parameters:

name

The name of the prompt in the registry. In Databricks, this is commonly a fully qualified Unity Catalog name, such as main.default.unity_airways_​cus⁠tomer_support, which keeps the prompt unambiguous across catalogs and schemas.

alias

The alias label you want to manage, such as staging or production. Think of this as the stable handle your application code should reference.

version

The integer prompt version that the alias should point to. This is the only thing you are “moving” when you promote or roll back.

Because aliases are mutable, you can promote a newer version by switching the alias to a different version, and your deployed application can keep loading the same alias (for example prompts:/...@production) without redeployment.

In this section, we keep the alias idea simple: it is your promotion lever. We will show how applications reference aliases cleanly in the next sections of this chapter.

Making prompts discoverable

Versioning tells you what changed. Tags tell you why it matters.

Databricks defines tags as version-specific, key-value pairs—a Git-like approach. In practice, good tagging is what makes a registry usable at scale, complementing versioning.

A useful tagging strategy should incorporate two types of tags:

Stable tags

These are relevant across multiple versions and include descriptors like use_case, owner, and language.

Change tags

These describe the specific changes in a particular version, such as improvement, risk, tested_with, or a brief hypothesis.

Tags are ideal for capturing the operational characteristics of prompts with low friction, offering examples such as tested_with, avg_latency_ms, team, and project. While not mandatory, these examples illustrate the mindset: tags capture operational context.

Searching prompts in Unity Catalog

You cannot manage what you cannot find. The registry provides search_prompts() for discovery.

While using a UC–backed registry, you must specify both catalog and schema in the filter string. Also, note the following limitations in Unity Catalog searches:

  • The only supported filter format is specifying the catalog and schema.

  • Name pattern filters are not supported.

  • Direct tag filtering is not supported.

That sounds restrictive, but it leads to a simple operational pattern:

  1. List prompts in a schema.

  2. Filter the returned list programmatically.

Here is an example:

import mlflow

# Required format: list all prompts in a catalog.schema
all_prompts = mlflow.genai.search_prompts(f"catalog = '{CATALOG}' AND schema = '{SCHEMA}'")

# Filter programmatically
ua_prompts = [p for p in all_prompts if "unity_airways" in p.name.lower()]
support_prompts = [p for p in all_prompts if p.tags.get("use_case") == "customer_support"]

This approach is explicitly recommended: get the list via search_prompts(...), then filter in Python. search_prompts() takes two arguments, filter_string and max_results:

filter_string (optional)

A SQL-like filter expression that tells MLflow which prompts to return. In a general MLflow Prompt Registry, you can filter by tags or other prompt fields, for example task='summarization'. In a Unity Catalog–backed Prompt Registry on Databricks, the filtering rules are stricter. You must specify both the catalog and schema, and that catalog = '...' AND schema = '...' pattern is the only supported filter format. This is why the recommended workflow is to list everything in the schema and then filter in Python. A practical naming convention makes this even easier. If all Unity Airways prompts start with unity_airways_, discovery becomes simple even without advanced server-side filters.

max_results (optional)

The maximum number of prompts to return from the search. Use it to keep listing operations fast and predictable, especially in shared workspaces with many prompts.

Deleting prompts

In Unity Catalog registries, you cannot delete a prompt if any versions of it still exist. The correct procedure is to first remove all existing versions using delete_prompt_version(), and only then can you delete the prompt itself.

That means cleanup typically looks like this:

from mlflow import MlflowClient
client = MlflowClient()
prompt_name = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support"

# Delete specific versions first (required for Unity Catalog)
client.delete_prompt_version(prompt_name, "1")
client.delete_prompt_version(prompt_name, "2")

# Then delete the prompt itself
client.delete_prompt(prompt_name)

delete_prompt_version() deletes one specific version of a prompt from the registry. It takes two parameters:

name

The prompt’s registry name to operate on. In a UC-backed registry, this is typically the fully qualified name, for example catalog.schema.prompt_name, so the client can unambiguously locate the prompt.

version

The version identifier to delete. MLflow expects this as a string in the API (for example "1"), and the method deletes only that single version.

The API is intentionally conservative. You delete versions one at a time, which reduces accidental “wipe everything” mistakes. The takeaway is not the code. It is the discipline: treat deletion as an administrative action, not a casual cleanup step. In most organizations, “delete” should be rarer than “deprecate,” and aliases make deprecation easy.

Using Prompts in Code

Storing prompts in the registry is only half the battle. The other half is making sure your application actually uses the registry consistently and in a way that stays maintainable as prompts evolve.

This section shows a simple, production-friendly pattern for consuming prompts from the MLflow Prompt Registry on Databricks (see Figure 3-6). The goals are practical:

  • You can reproduce behavior during development by pinning a prompt version.

  • You can update behavior in production by switching an alias, without changing application code.

  • You render template variables safely and fail when something is incompatible.

Loading a Prompt

To enable dynamic updates without needing to redeploy application code, we recommend that you load prompts via aliases instead of using hardcoded version numbers. This approach clearly communicates the intent: use a stable alias, like production, and update the deployed behavior by reassigning that alias to the desired newer version. A rule of thumb would be:

  • Use a specific version when you are developing, testing, or debugging and you want deterministic reproduction.

  • Use an alias when you are running in production or any environment where promotion and rollback should not require code changes.

This is the same mindset you use for software dependencies: pin versions for tests, use controlled release channels for production.

Loading a prompt by alias

The production path is defined by aliases. Databricks specifies the alias URI syntax as prompts:/{catalog}.{schema}.{prompt_name}@{alias}.

Here is a short example:

import mlflow

prompt_name = "main.default.unity_airways_customer_support"
prompt_prod = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(f"prompts:/{prompt_name}@production")

print(prompt_prod.name, prompt_prod.version)

A deployed application should not hardcode the alias either. Databricks provides a reference pattern that reads PROMPT_URI and PROMPT_ALIAS from environment variables and then constructs the prompt URI accordingly.

Here is that pattern, adapted to the Unity Airways example:

import os
mlflow.set_registry_uri("databricks-uc")

def load_runtime_prompt() -> object:
    prompt_alias = os.getenv("PROMPT_ALIAS", "production")
    prompt_uri = os.getenv("PROMPT_URI", f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA} \
    .unity_airways_customer_support")
    uri = f"prompts:/{prompt_uri}@{prompt_alias}"
    return mlflow.genai.load_prompt(uri)

prompt = load_runtime_prompt()
print(f"Loaded {prompt.name} v{prompt.version}")

This gives you a clean operational knob: deploy the same code everywhere, but choose whether it points to staging or production via configuration.

Loading a prompt by version

There are two common ways to load a specific version: by URI (prompts:/.../​ver⁠sion) or by providing name and version.

The URI form is easy to standardize:

import mlflow

prompt_name = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support"
prompt_v2 = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(f"prompts:/{prompt_name}/2")

print(prompt_v2.name, prompt_v2.version)

load_prompt() loads a prompt version from the Prompt Registry. You can point it at an explicit version or at an alias-based URI so your application can follow promotions without a redeploy. The parameters are:

name_or_uri

The prompt identifier to load. This can be either:

  • A prompt name (for example, a fully qualified Unity Catalog name like main.default.unity_airways_customer_support)

  • A prompt URI, such as prompts:/my_prompt/1 for a specific version, or an alias URI like prompts:/main.default.unity_airways_customer_​sup⁠port@production. Databricks documents the alias URI format as prompts:/{catalog}.{schema}.{prompt_name}@{alias}.

version

The version to load when name_or_uri is a name. It is required if you want a specific version by name, and it is not allowed when you pass a URI.

allow_missing

If allow_missing=True, load_prompt returns None instead of raising an exception when the prompt is not found. This is useful when you intentionally treat prompts as optional. For most production systems, missing prompts should be treated as a configuration error, not as a normal scenario.

cache_ttl_seconds

Controls client-side caching for loaded prompts. If you do not set it, MLflow uses environment-variable defaults. Alias-based prompts typically default to a short TTL (for example, 60 seconds), while version-based loads default to no TTL. Set it to 0 to bypass caching and always fetch the latest mapping from the registry.

Rendering Template Variables with format()

Loading a prompt gives you a template. Using it requires rendering variables. Databricks examples show the standard pattern: load a prompt, then call prompt.format(...) with keyword arguments for each variable.

Here’s a simple example:

formatted = prompt.format(question="Can I change my flight tomorrow?")

This looks harmless, but it is where many production prompt failures begin. Prompt versions evolve. Variables get renamed. New variables appear. If your application does not catch incompatibilities early, you end up with either runtime exceptions or silently broken prompts that produce nonsense.

A small wrapper makes this safer:

from typing import Any, Dict

def render_prompt(prompt_obj, variables: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    try:
        return prompt_obj.format(**variables)
    except Exception as e:
        raise ValueError(
            f"Prompt formatting failed for '{getattr(prompt_obj, 'name', '<unknown>')}' "
            f"(version={getattr(prompt_obj, 'version', '<unknown>')}). "
            f"Provided keys: {sorted(list(variables.keys()))}"
        ) from e

text = render_prompt(prompt, {"question": "Do I get a refund if I miss my flight?"})
print(text)

The execution of this code prints the following output text:

You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Rules:
- If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or exceptions.

Customer question: Do I get a refund if I miss my flight?

Write a concise answer (max 120 words).

This is not fancy, but it turns a confusing runtime error into something you can actually fix quickly.

Making the Model Call: A Minimal Databricks Pattern

Once you have a formatted prompt, you send it to a model endpoint. Databricks commonly uses an OpenAI-compatible client obtained via the Databricks SDK, which works cleanly with model serving endpoints.

Here is a minimal end-to-end call:

from databricks.sdk import WorkspaceClient

w = WorkspaceClient()
client = w.serving_endpoints.get_open_ai_client()

prompt = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(
    f"prompts:/{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support@production"
)
content = prompt.format(question="Can I change my flight tomorrow?")
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="databricks-gpt-oss-120b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
    temperature=0.1,
    max_tokens=350,
)
answer = resp.choices[0].message.content
print(answer)

Here are a few operational defaults to consider for a customer support agent:

  • Keep the temperature low for consistency.

  • Set max_tokens to prevent unexpectedly long outputs.

  • Log the prompt name and version so you can correlate behaviors to prompt changes.

Error-Handling Patterns and Gotchas

A registry makes changes easier, and that also means it makes mistakes easier. The goal is to add a few guardrails so mistakes fail loudly and predictably, instead of showing up as strange customer-facing behavior.

At runtime, always record which prompt was used. If a customer reports, “It said I could get a refund,” you want to trace that output back to a specific prompt version. The simplest habit is logging the prompt name and version whenever you generate a response; for example, you could use the following during development, but a proper application logger in production:

print(f"Prompt used: {prompt.name} v{prompt.version}")

Also avoid loading prompts on every request unless you truly need it. A common pattern is to load the prompt at startup, refresh it on a schedule or after a deployment restart, and keep runtime configuration stable. This keeps latency predictable and reduces failure points, while still letting aliases do their job because promotion can be paired with a refresh or restart.

If you use allow_missing=True with load_prompt, only do it when you have a conservative fallback prompt and you log clearly that the fallback was used; otherwise, missing prompts can silently degrade behavior.

Finally, watch out for a few common gotchas that cause avoidable pain:

  • Hardcoding versions in production: it works, but it defeats the entire purpose of aliases and makes rollbacks a deployment event.

  • Changing prompt variables without updating callers: this is the most common source of runtime failures. Use a formatting wrapper and test with the exact prompt version you plan to promote.

  • Assuming a prompt is “just text”: once prompts affect user outcomes, treat updates like releases. The registry makes that easy, but it does not enforce discipline by itself.

With these patterns, prompts become a managed dependency rather than a hardcoded string, and your application stays stable even as prompt behavior evolves. Next, we will compare prompt versions on a fixed dataset so promotions are driven by evidence, not intuition.

Evaluating and Comparing Prompt Versions

Now you are familiar with versioning and aliases. Just to recap, prompt versioning gives you history, and aliases let you promote them safely. Evaluation is the missing ingredient that turns “I like version 2 better” into “Version 2 is measurably better on the behaviors we care about.”

On Databricks, evaluating and comparing prompt versions is achieved using MLflow’s evaluation framework. The core idea is straightforward: create prompt versions, build an evaluation dataset with expected facts, and compare versions side-by-side. This chapter keeps evaluation intentionally narrow as we will cover evaluation strategy for GenAI applications in detail in Chapter 6. Here, we focus on one question: which prompt version should we promote to staging and then to production?

The process has three moving parts:

  • A fixed evaluation dataset that represents real questions and edge cases

  • A repeatable way to run a prompt version

  • A comparison step that summarizes results so you can make a promotion decision

What matters is consistency. If you change both the prompt and the dataset at the same time, you are no longer comparing versions. You are running a different experiment.

Building a Prompt Evaluation Dataset

A prompt evaluation dataset is not meant to be huge. It is meant to be representative.

For the Unity Airways example, the “gotcha” questions are predictable: refunds, missed flights, cancellations, flight changes, and anything that tempts the model to invent policy. Your dataset should include a healthy dose of those, plus a few straightforward questions so you do not optimize only for scary scenarios.

A dataset should have the following fields:

inputs

What your prompt receives (for this chapter, we will keep it to question)

expectations

What a good answer should include, expressed as a short list of expected facts

That expected-facts approach works well for customer support because good answers often vary in wording, but they should still include certain core ideas: “eligibility depends on fare rules,” “I need your booking reference,” “I can’t confirm a refund without fare conditions,” and so on.

Here is a dataset creation pattern that stores the dataset in Unity Catalog and populates it with a few initial cases:

EVAL_DATASET_NAME = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.ua_support_prompt_eval"
eval_dataset = mlflow.genai.datasets.create_dataset(
    name=EVAL_DATASET_NAME
)
evaluation_examples = [
    {
        "inputs": {
            "question": "My flight is tomorrow. Can I change it to next week?"
        },
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Eligibility depends on fare rules or fare type",
                "May involve a change fee or fare difference",
                "Ask for booking reference or fare details if missing"
            ]
        }
    },
    {
        "inputs": {
            "question": "I missed my flight due to traffic. Do I get a refund?"
        },
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Refund eligibility depends on fare rules",
                "Do not promise a refund without checking ticket conditions",
                "Provide next steps to verify eligibility"
            ]
        }
    },
    {
        "inputs": {
            "question": "My flight was canceled. Can I rebook for free?"
        },
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Rebooking depends on disruption policy",
                "Ask for booking details if needed",
                "Avoid claiming blanket waivers without evidence"
            ]
        }
    },
]
eval_dataset = eval_dataset.merge_records(evaluation_examples)
print(f"Added {len(evaluation_examples)} examples to {EVAL_DATASET_NAME}")

This code helps to create a small evaluation dataset and register it in the Unity Catalog, as you can see in Figure 3-7.

This dataset is deliberately small so you can validate the workflow quickly. In practice, you will grow it over time. The most valuable additions are usually not more “average” questions. Two tips help keep “expected facts” precise and evaluable:

  • Write facts as checkable statements, not aspirations. “Be helpful” is not testable. Define behaviors you can verify in the output.

    • Example (good): “If refund eligibility depends on fare rules, ask for fare type and booking reference before stating eligibility.”

    • Example (good): “When the user asks for compensation, cite the relevant policy section or state that you cannot determine eligibility without flight number and disruption reason.”

    • Example (bad): “Be clear and friendly.”

    • Example (bad): “Give the best answer you can.”

  • Include hard cases where the model is tempted to guess. These are the scenarios that reveal whether the prompt enforces honesty, policy compliance, and disciplined clarification.

    • Example (refund temptation): “My flight is tomorrow and I want a full refund. I bought the cheapest ticket. Can you confirm I’ll get 100% back?”
      Expected behavior: Ask for fare type and ticket conditions, avoid promises, and explain what can and cannot be confirmed.

    • Example (compensation temptation): “My flight was delayed 4 hours. Am I entitled to $600 compensation under EU rules?”
      Expected behavior: Request route details, operating carrier, cause of delay, and ticket info, and avoid quoting entitlements without jurisdiction confirmation.

Over time, treat this dataset as a living artifact. Keep adding these high-leverage examples, retire obsolete ones when policies change, and make each expected behavior specific enough that a reviewer can say “pass” or “fail” without debate.

Creating Prompt Versions to Compare

When you have multiple prompt versions, you can register them in MLflow for comparison. The specifics of the prompt content are up to you, but the important part is that versions represent different approaches you want to test. A good first comparison is usually “minimal prompt” versus “constrained prompt”:

  • v1: Short prompt, low instruction

  • v2: Clear constraints around missing details, speculation, and brevity

Here we will use the same prompts that we registered under prompt_name earlier in this chapter. Now that we have the versions ready and an evaluation dataset prepared, the next step is to run the comparison using MLflow’s evaluation framework to objectively determine which prompt performs best on our defined metrics, and then promote the winner.

Running Comparative Evaluation

We need a consistent way to run each prompt version. The pattern is always the same:

  1. Load a specific prompt version from Prompt Registry.

  2. Render variables with .format(...).

  3. Send rendered text to an LLM hosted by the Databricks Foundation Model API.

  4. Return the output in a consistent shape so evaluation can score it.

We will use Databricks Model Serving exclusively via the OpenAI-compatible client provided by the Databricks SDK. For example:

client = w.serving_endpoints.get_open_ai_client()

def create_support_function(prompt_name: str, version: int):
    """
    Returns a predict_fn for a specific prompt version.
    The function returns a dict so evaluation can read outputs consistently.
    """
    def answer_question(question: str) -> dict:
        prompt = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(
            name_or_uri=f"prompts:/{prompt_name}/{version}"
        )
        formatted = prompt.format(question=question)

        resp = client.chat.completions.create(
            model="databricks-gpt-oss-120b",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": formatted}],
            temperature=0.1,
            max_tokens=350,
        )
        return {"response": resp.choices[0].message.content}
    return answer_question

Next, run evaluation for each version. The evaluation metrics you choose should be minimal at first. A good starting point is correctness against expected facts because it aligns directly with your dataset structure. Here is an example:

from mlflow.genai.scorers import Correctness

checks = [
    Correctness(),  # Uses expected_facts in the dataset expectations
]

results = {}
for version in [v1.version, v2.version]:
    print(f"Evaluating version {version}")
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"ua_support_v{version}_eval"):
        mlflow.log_param("prompt_name", prompt_name)
        mlflow.log_param("prompt_version", version)
        mlflow.log_param("eval_dataset", EVAL_DATASET_NAME)

        eval_results = mlflow.genai.evaluate(
            predict_fn=create_support_function(prompt_name, version),
            data=eval_dataset,
            scorers=checks,
        )

        results[f"v{version}"] = eval_results
        print(f"Correctness: {eval_results.metrics.get('correctness/mean', 0):.2f}")

After executing this code, you should be able to see that two evaluation runs in your MLflow experiment, as you can see in Figure 3-8.

This gives you a like-for-like comparison: same dataset, same model endpoint, different prompt version.

Comparing Results and Choosing a Winner

Once you have evaluation runs for multiple prompt versions, there are two ways to compare them: programmatically in a notebook and visually in the MLflow UI. In practice, teams often do both. The notebook view is great for quick iteration and automation, while the UI view is great for review discussions because everyone can look at the same evidence without rerunning code.

Compare in the MLflow UI

After your evaluation runs are logged, open the MLflow experiment and navigate to the runs created for each prompt version. In the runs table, filter or group by the prompt_version parameter so the candidates sit next to each other. Then use the built-in comparison view to compare metrics across the selected runs, as you can see in Figure 3-9.

Once you select the runs for the versions you are comparing, compare their key metrics (for example, correctness/mean) side-by-side. Figure 3-10 shows this comparison.

Compare programmatically

If you want a quick numeric summary in notebooks or CI-style checks, keep the programmatic comparison. Start simple with a single metric, then add more checks only when you have a clear reason. Here is an example:

print("\n=== Version Comparison ===")
for version_label, result in results.items():
    correctness = result.metrics.get("correctness/mean", 0)
    print(f"{version_label}: correctness={correctness:.2f}")

best = max(results.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1].metrics.get("correctness/mean", 0))
print(f"\nBest version by correctness: {best[0]}")

After executing this code, you should be able to see the following output:

=== Version Comparison ===
v1: correctness=0.33
v2: correctness=0.67

Best version by correctness: v2

As you may have already noticed, it’s aligned with the observations we had on the MLflow UI.

Decide promotion with a clear rule

Whether you compare in the UI or in code, the promotion rule should be explainable and consistent. A good starting rule is: promote the version with higher correctness, as long as it does not introduce obvious regressions when you spot-check a handful of edge cases.

Interpreting the results is still a product decision, not a math contest:

  • If v2 improves correctness but gets too long, tighten the word limit and create v3.

  • If v2 improves correctness but starts asking unnecessary clarifying questions, refine the “ask one clarifying question” rule and add a few dataset examples where the correct behavior is to answer directly.

  • If v2 regresses, do not promote; instead, iterate.

Once you have a winner, you can move the staging alias first, validate quickly, then move the alias to production.

Prompt Optimization

Prompt optimization is an automated way to improve a prompt template using data and measurable criteria, rather than relying only on manual edits and intuition. Instead of guessing which wording will help, you provide (1) representative inputs, (2) what a good answer must contain, and (3) a budget for exploration. The optimizer proposes an improved prompt template. You still review it, register it as a new version, and promote it only after it performs well in your version comparison workflow.

This section shows how to run optimization in a disciplined way that fits the prompt lifecycle you already established: versioned prompts, fixed datasets, and alias-based promotion.

When Optimization Helps

Optimization is most useful when you can define “better” in a way you can test. Customer support prompts are often a good fit because improvement goals are concrete:

  • Include required facts, such as “eligibility depends on fare rules.”

  • Avoid speculation about fees and waivers.

  • Ask for missing booking details when needed.

  • Keep answers concise and consistent in structure.

Optimization is less useful when the root issue is missing context rather than prompt wording. If the prompt is guessing because the application never supplies fare rules or disruption policy, optimization will mostly produce longer prompts that still cannot access the missing information. In that case, improve the inputs first, then optimize the prompt.

Multiple Techniques Through a Single MLflow Interface

MLflow exposes prompt optimization through a unified API (mlflow.genai.​opti⁠mize_prompts) and supports multiple built-in optimizers, while keeping the interface stable so you can swap techniques without rewriting your application.

As of this writing, MLflow supports two first-class approaches:

GEPA (via GepaPromptOptimizer)

An iterative approach that refines prompts using reflection and feedback, designed for data-driven improvement when you have a meaningful dataset and clear metrics.

Metaprompting (via MetaPromptOptimizer)

Restructures prompts to be more systematic. It can run in zero-shot mode (no training data) or few-shot mode (learns from your examples).

Under the hood, these optimizers build on open source techniques and packages. For example, the GEPA library is available as an open source project and is referenced as an integration target for mlflow.genai.optimize_prompts(). Later we will discuss how to use a GEPA prompt optimizer using a comprehensive example.

In practice, you can treat MLflow as the integration layer that standardizes:

  • How prompts are versioned and swapped (Prompt Registry)

  • How candidates are scored (scorers and evaluation datasets)

  • How results are tracked and compared (runs, metrics, and version lineage)

  • How winners move to staging or production (aliases)

A Unity Airways Optimization Workflow

The optimization workflow has four steps:

  1. Register a baseline prompt in the Prompt Registry.

  2. Define a predict function that loads the prompt from the registry.

  3. Provide training examples with inputs and expected facts.

  4. Run optimization to produce an improved prompt template candidate.

Step 1: Register a baseline prompt

Establish a simple, baseline prompt version to serve as the “current behavior” and stable reference point. This initial prompt needs minimum guardrails (e.g., do not speculate on fees, ask for missing details, keep it short). Once registered, the baseline is versioned and immutable, allowing meaningful comparison for future changes. Each improvement becomes a new, clearly committed version. Here is an example:

PROMPT_NAME = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_support_answer"

baseline = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name=PROMPT_NAME,
    template="""\
You are a customer support assistant for Unity Airways.

Rules:
- If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or refund eligibility.
- Keep the answer under 120 words.

Customer question:
{{question}}

Answer:
""",
    commit_message="v1: baseline support answer prompt"
)

print(f"Baseline prompt: {baseline.name} v{baseline.version}")
Note

A requirement is that the prediction function must load the prompt from the registry and render it with PromptVersion.​for⁠mat(). If you hardcode the prompt string inside the function, the optimizer cannot influence anything meaningful.

Step 2: Define a prediction function

This function loads a specific prompt version, formats it, and sends it to a Databricks FMAPI endpoint via the OpenAI-compatible client from the Databricks SDK. Here is an example:

from databricks_openai import DatabricksOpenAI

openai_client = DatabricksOpenAI()

# Define your prediction function
def predict_fn(question: str) -> str:
    prompt = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(f"prompts:/{PROMPT_NAME}/{baseline.version}")
    content = prompt.format(question=question)

    resp = openai_client.chat.completions.create(
        model="databricks-gpt-oss-120b",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=350,
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content

Step 3: Provide training examples with expected facts

Training examples should look like the questions you actually get, not like the questions you wish customers would ask. Include edge cases where the model is tempted to guess. For example:

train_dataset = [
    {
        "inputs": {"question": "My flight is tomorrow. Can I change it to next week?"},
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Eligibility depends on fare rules or fare type",
                "May involve a change fee or fare difference",
                "Ask for booking reference or fare details if missing"
            ]
        }
    },
    {
        "inputs": {"question": "I missed my flight due to traffic. Do I get a refund?"},
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Refund eligibility depends on fare rules",
                "Do not promise a refund without checking ticket conditions",
                "Provide next steps to verify eligibility"
            ]
        }
    },
    {
        "inputs": {"question": "My flight was canceled. Can I rebook for free?"},
        "expectations": {
            "expected_facts": [
                "Rebooking depends on disruption policy",
                "Ask for booking details if needed",
                "Avoid claiming blanket waivers without evidence"
            ]
        }
    },
]

Step 4: Run optimization and inspect the candidate template

Now that you have a baseline prompt, a prediction function that actually uses the registry prompt, and a small but representative training set, you can run optimization to generate a candidate prompt template. Think of this candidate as a proposed rewrite that is trying to satisfy your expected facts more reliably. It is not “the new truth.” It is a draft produced by an automated process that still needs human review and validation.

When the optimization finishes, you should inspect the candidate template with two hats on:

Quality hat

Does the candidate read like something you would actually want in production? Is it clear, consistent, and aligned with your support posture?

Risk hat

Did it become overly verbose, overly cautious, or strangely repetitive? Does it introduce new instructions that could cause unexpected behavior?

It is common for the candidate to become more explicit than your baseline. That is often how reliability improves: the template may spell out constraints and decision rules more clearly. The question is whether the extra verbosity is worth the stability gain in your environment.

Run optimization and extract the candidate template:

from mlflow.genai.optimize import GepaPromptOptimizer
from mlflow.genai.scorers import Correctness

result = mlflow.genai.optimize_prompts(
    predict_fn=predict_fn,
    train_data=train_dataset,
    prompt_uris=[baseline.uri],
    optimizer=GepaPromptOptimizer(
reflection_model="databricks:/databricks-gpt-oss-120b",
max_metric_calls=20,
),
    scorers=[Correctness(model="databricks:/databricks-gpt-oss-120b")],
)

candidate = result.optimized_prompts[0]
print("=== Candidate optimized template ===")
print(candidate.template)

What the GepaPromptOptimizer parameters do:

reflection_model

The model GEPA uses to propose edits to your template. This is your “prompt editor” model, and it does not need to be the same model you serve in production. Pick something that is strong at instruction-following and rewriting, and cost-effective enough to run multiple iterations.

max_metric_calls

Your optimization budget. It caps how many evaluation calls are made during optimization. Larger values explore more candidates and can improve results, but they increase runtime and cost. The default is 100, so set it lower when you are validating the workflow, then raise it after everything is wired correctly.

display_progress_bar (optional)

Shows a progress bar while optimization runs. Useful in notebooks, noisy in logs. The default value is False.

gepa_kwargs (optional)

Advanced pass-through settings for the underlying GEPA implementation. Leave it alone until you have a reason to tune the search behavior.

After printing the template, do a quick “sanity scan” before you register anything:

  • Does it still enforce “ask exactly one clarifying question” when details are missing?

  • Does it still avoid inventing fees, waivers, or eligibility?

  • Does it still keep the response concise, or did it accidentally encourage long explanations?

At this stage, a quick UI review is also helpful because it makes it easy for the candidate to discuss with teammates.

If the candidate looks reasonable, the next step is to register it as a new prompt version and then run the same evaluation and comparison workflow you used in the previous section. That is the moment the candidate earns the right to become staging, and eventually production. Figure 3-11 illustrates this prompt optimization flow.

How Optimization Works Under the Hood

At a high level, prompt optimization is a search loop wrapped around your existing application logic. For the best outcome, adhere to the following workflow steps:

  1. You define the target behavior and how to measure it. You provide an evaluation dataset (inputs plus expected outputs or expectations) and scorers that turn model outputs into metrics you can optimize.

  2. You run your predict function. MLflow asks you for a predict_fn that executes your chain or agent. That function loads the prompt from the Prompt Registry and formats it via PromptVersion.format(), so the optimizer can swap in candidate templates while keeping everything else constant.

  3. The optimizer proposes candidate prompt edits within a budget. Each algorithm has its own strategy, but they all operate under explicit limits such as a maximum number of metric calls. This is what keeps “try everything” from turning into an unbounded spend.

  4. Candidates are evaluated, compared, and selected. MLflow runs the candidates against your dataset using your predict_fn, computes scores, aggregates them, and picks the best-performing template according to your criteria. The result is returned as an optimized prompt object that you can review and register like any other version.

The point is that optimization does not replace your lifecycle. It accelerates the “propose candidate” step, but you still rely on evaluation, comparison, and controlled promotion to decide what ships.

Keeping Optimization Practical

Optimization can get slow or expensive if you feed it a large dataset and give it an unconstrained budget, so start small and scale deliberately. A good first pass is a compact, representative training set that covers your highest-risk behaviors; then expand coverage only after you confirm the workflow produces sensible candidates. If runtime is high, reduce the number of examples and cap the budget, or switch to a faster reflection model so iteration stays practical.

Two common failure modes are worth watching for:

  • The candidate prompt becomes more complicated but does not improve results, which usually means your training examples do not reflect the behaviors you actually care about or your expected facts are too vague to guide meaningful improvement.

  • The optimizer appears to run but the prompt never changes, which is often caused by a predict_fn that does not load the prompt from the registry and does not use .format(), leaving nothing real to optimize.

When you do get a promising candidate, keep the finishing move consistent and boring:

  • Compare the optimized version against the current best using the same evaluation workflow from the previous section.

  • Assign the winner to staging first.

  • Promote to production only after staging validation.

  • Keep rollback trivial by knowing the previous production version.

Optimization can generate candidates faster, but release discipline stays exactly the same.

Integrating Prompts into Applications

Prompts become operational the moment they affect customer-facing behavior. At that point, a prompt edit is not just changing text. It is changing product behavior. The goal of integration is to make those behavior changes safe, repeatable, and reversible, without forcing an application to redeploy every time you refine wording.

A reliable integration pattern has two ideas:

  • Immutable prompt versions capture exactly what changed and when.

  • Aliases (like staging and production) act as stable pointers that your application can reference.

Your application should load prompts by alias, not by version number. That way, the application stays stable while the alias controls which prompt version is active.

A practical release workflow for prompts looks like this:

  1. Publish a new prompt version (manual edit or optimization output).

  2. Point staging to the candidate version.

  3. Validate using your evaluation workflow and a quick staging sanity check.

  4. Move production to the candidate version.

  5. Keep rollback trivial by remembering the previous production version.

This is the same safety model you use for application configuration: change in a controlled environment first, promote when it proves itself, and keep a fast rollback path.

Publishing Versions and Assigning Aliases

Start by registering a baseline prompt and then creating a revised version. Registering again with the same prompt name creates a new version, which is exactly what you want: history stays intact and comparisons stay meaningful.

The following snippet creates two versions of a Unity Airways support prompt and assigns aliases so staging points to the newer candidate while production remains on the known-good version:

PROMPT = f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support"

# Version 1: baseline
v1 = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name=PROMPT,
    template="""\
You are a Unity Airways customer support assistant.
Customer question: {{question}}
""",
    commit_message="v1: minimal support prompt",
)

# Version 2: safer, more constrained behavior
v2 = mlflow.genai.register_prompt(
    name=PROMPT,
    template="""\
You are a careful Unity Airways customer support assistant.

Rules:
- If key details are missing, ask exactly one clarifying question.
- Do not invent fees, waivers, or refund eligibility.
- Keep the answer under 120 words.

Customer question:
{{question}}

Answer:
""",
    commit_message="v2: add safety constraints and brevity limit",
)

# Aliases control rollout
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name=PROMPT, alias="staging", version=v2.version)
mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(name=PROMPT, alias="production", version=v1.version)

print(f"Staging -> v{v2.version}, Production -> v{v1.version}")

At this point, you have created a clean separation between “what is in the registry” and “what is live for customers.” The candidate exists, but it is only staged.

Referencing Aliases in Your Application

Now we make the application consume prompts in a way that supports safe releases. The simplest approach is to have the app build a prompt URI at runtime from environment variables:

PROMPT_URI

Unity Catalog prompt name (e.g., main.default.unity_airways_customer_​sup⁠port)

PROMPT_ALIAS

Which alias to load (default to production)

This lets you deploy the same code everywhere and switch behavior by configuration alone. In production, you typically set PROMPT_ALIAS=production. In staging, you set PROMPT_ALIAS=staging. Everything else remains identical.

End-to-End “Thin Slice”

Once you have a prompt object, you render it with .format(...) and send the resulting text to an LLM. In this chapter, we will use Databricks FMAPI via the OpenAI-compatible client provided by the Databricks SDK. The key is that the prompt comes from the registry and is selected via alias, so your model call is always paired with a known prompt version.

The example that follows shows an end-to-end function that answers a customer question using whatever alias is configured in the environment:

from databricks_openai import DatabricksOpenAI

openai_client = DatabricksOpenAI()

def answer_customer(question: str) -> str:
    prompt_name = os.getenv("PROMPT_URI", f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA} \
    .unity_airways_customer_support")
    alias = os.getenv("PROMPT_ALIAS", "production")

    # Load the prompt by alias
    prompt = mlflow.genai.load_prompt(f"prompts:/{prompt_name}@{alias}")

    # Render the template variables
    content = prompt.format(question=question)

    # Call the model serving endpoint
    resp = openai_client.chat.completions.create(
        model="databricks-gpt-oss-120b",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}],
        temperature=0.1,
        max_tokens=350,
    )
    return resp.choices[0].message.content

print(answer_customer("My flight is tomorrow. Can I change it to next week?"))

This “thin slice” is intentionally simple. It proves the integration contract: the application reads configuration, loads a prompt by alias, formats variables, and sends a request. You can wrap this with a web API, a Databricks App, or a batch job later. The release mechanism stays the same.

Promoting to Production and Rolling Back Safely

Once your evaluation results look good and staging behavior is acceptable, promotion is a single alias reassignment. That is the whole point of using aliases in application code.

First, promote by moving the production alias to the candidate version:

mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support",
    alias="production",
    version=v2.version
)

If anything unexpected happens, rollback is equally simple. Move production back to the previous version:

mlflow.genai.set_prompt_alias(
    name=f"{CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.unity_airways_customer_support",
    alias="production",
    version=v1.version
)

Two operational habits make this safer:

  • Record the previous production version before promotion, so rollback is immediate.

  • Keep the promotion from staging to production explicit, even if your team is small. It prevents accidental releases.

A small amount of discipline prevents most prompt integration incidents, focusing on practices like logging the prompt name and version at runtime to aid debugging, ensuring quick failure on template incompatibility during staging, and avoiding hardcoded versions in production in favor of dynamic aliases. Treating alias moves as formal release actions, even when the underlying code hasn’t changed, requires a lightweight checklist covering evaluation results, prompt text review, and a clear rollback plan. These practices are all essential for stable and production-ready GenAI applications.

Conclusion and Key Takeaways

Prompt engineering is an engineering problem requiring the same discipline as code: version control, safe releases, reproducibility, and ownership.

This chapter outlined the end-to-end prompt lifecycle on Databricks, starting with fundamentals: prompts must be explicit about scope, constraints, and how to handle missing information. Ambiguity is common in scenarios like customer support, so a good prompt ensures a safe posture: ask for missing details, avoid guessing, and keep the output concise.

We then covered prompt management using the MLflow Prompt Registry in Unity Catalog, which provides immutable, versioned prompts with metadata for collaboration. This enables tracking changes and what is running, and allows prompt improvement without fragile application strings.

Next, we made prompt usage predictable by loading from the registry and rendering with variables, separating application logic from prompt behavior. This separation enables prompt evolution, as template incompatibility issues are found in staging before impacting customers.

Finally, we discussed tightening the feedback loop. Comparing prompt versions on fixed datasets enables evidence-based selection. Automatic prompt optimization accelerates iteration but must follow the same discipline: generate, validate, and safely promote. Automation speeds up the process; it doesn’t skip steps.

The core theme is making prompt changes routine, measurable, and reversible. Adopting this early makes prompt engineering a reliable part of development, not a source of surprises.

Key takeaways from this chapter include:

  • Treat prompts as production assets, not notebook text. They affect customer outcomes.

  • Write prompts as contracts with clear scope, explicit constraints, and safe handling of missing information.

  • Use the MLflow Prompt Registry as the source of truth. Keep prompts versioned, tagged, and governed in Unity Catalog.

  • Embrace immutability. Every meaningful edit is a new prompt version, which makes comparisons and rollbacks reliable.

  • Use aliases for deployment. Application code should reference production and staging, not numeric versions.

  • Load and format prompts consistently in code, and fail fast when variables or templates become incompatible.

  • Compare prompt versions on a stable evaluation dataset before promotion. Keep the dataset fixed during comparisons.

  • Use automatic prompt optimization to propose improvements, but only promote what proves itself under the same checks.

  • Keep releases reversible. Promoting and rolling back prompt behavior should be a pointer change, rather than a redeployment process.
